title: More tenses for B2
intro: Tenses that build on the B1 guide: present perfect simple and continuous, past perfect, the future continuous and future perfect, and past habits.

sources.label: British Council: Present perfect simple and continuous
British Council: Future continuous and future perfect

sections.title: Present perfect simple and continuous
sections.summary: Both link the past to the present. The continuous form stresses the activity and how long it lasts, the simple form stresses the result.

tables.caption: Simple and continuous
head: form
structure
example
rows: I have been writing emails all morning.
How long have you been waiting?

uses: Continuous: an activity that started in the past and continues, or has just stopped with a visible result: Your eyes are red. Have you been crying?
Simple: the result or the number: I have read ten books this year.
For and since go with both forms: She has lived / has been living here since 2019.
Do not use the continuous with stative verbs such as know, like, believe: I have known her for years.

examples.text: We have been waiting for an hour.
He has painted the kitchen. (it is finished)
She has been painting the kitchen all day.

mistakes.wrong: I have been knowing her for years.
mistakes.right: I have known her for years.

mistakes.wrong: I have been reading three books this month.
mistakes.right: I have read three books this month.
mistakes.why: A number points to a result, use the simple form.

checks.question: Complete: How long ___ (you / learn) English?
checks.explanation: A period of time, the activity continues.

checks.question: Complete: I ___ (finish) my homework. Now I can go out.

sections.title: Past perfect
sections.summary: Use the past perfect for a past action that happened before another past action or time.

tables.caption: Past perfect
head: form
structure
example
rows: She had left when I arrived.

uses: Show which of two past events happened first: When I got to the station, the train had gone.
Reported speech: He said he had finished.
Third conditional: If I had known, I would have come.
After by the time, before, after, when, because and until.
If the order is clear from the words after or before, you can use the past simple: After he left, I went to bed.

examples.text: I had never seen snow before I went to Canada.
By the time we arrived, the film had started.
She was tired because she had worked all night.

mistakes.wrong: When I arrived, they already left.
mistakes.right: When I arrived, they had already left.

checks.question: Complete: When she called, I ___ (already / go) to bed.
Complete: He felt sick because he ___ (eat) too much.
checks.explanation: The eating came before the feeling.

sections.title: Future continuous and future perfect
sections.summary: Use these two forms to talk about activities or results at a time in the future.

tables.caption: Two future forms
head: form
structure
example
rows: This time tomorrow I will be flying to Rome.
By Friday I will have finished the report.
Will you be using the car tonight?
I won't have finished by then.

uses: Future continuous: an activity in progress at a future time: At eight tonight I will be watching the match.
A polite way to ask about plans: Will you be coming to the party?
Future perfect: something is complete before a future time: By 2030 she will have graduated.
Time words with future perfect: by, by the time, before, by then.

examples.text: In ten years I will be living in another country.
They will have built the bridge by next summer.
Will you be going to the shop? Could you buy some milk?

mistakes.wrong: By next year I will finish my studies.
mistakes.right: By next year I will have finished my studies.
mistakes.why: By + a future time needs future perfect.

mistakes.wrong: I will be knowing the results on Monday.
mistakes.right: I will know the results on Monday.

checks.question: Complete: This time next week I ___ (lie) on a beach.
checks.explanation: An activity in progress in the future.

checks.question: Complete: By June she ___ (finish) the course.

sections.title: Past habits: used to, would and the past simple
sections.summary: There are three ways to talk about past habits and states. Choose the correct one.

tables.caption: Past habits
head: form
use
example
rows: I used to live in Madrid. She used to be shy.
Every summer we would go to the beach.
a completed action or a clear time
I lived in Madrid for six years.
I am used to getting up early.

uses: Used to talks about something that is not true any more.
Questions and negatives use use to: Did you use to play? I didn't use to like fish.
Would cannot describe a state: I used to have a bike, not I would have a bike.
Use the past simple when you give a number of times or a period of time: We went there three times.
Be used to + -ing means be accustomed. It is different from used to + base form.

examples.text: He used to smoke, but he stopped last year.
When I was a child, we would visit my grandparents every Sunday.
I am not used to the cold weather.
examples.note: Be used to + noun or -ing = familiar with.

mistakes.wrong: Did you used to live here?
mistakes.right: Did you use to live here?

mistakes.wrong: I would be shy as a child.
mistakes.right: I used to be shy as a child.

mistakes.wrong: I used to going to the gym.
mistakes.right: I am used to going to the gym.
mistakes.why: Used to + base form is for the past.

checks.question: Complete: When I was young I ___ (used to / would) have a dog.
Complete: She ___ (be) used to living alone now.
